backups_continuity.title: Sysadmin 4 — Backups, Recovery & Business Continuity
backups_continuity.desc: Backups and continuity on the managed platform: the two custodies; the database-plus-files completeness rule; RPO and RTO held in writing; the Download Backups page with the daily presence check and the monthly off-platform copy; the three restore paths with sets named by timestamp; the monthly restore drill and the annual full dress; the before-change backup with the no-timestamp-no-run reflex; and the four-scenario continuity runbook with degraded tills and governed re-entry.

lessons.title: Chapter 1 — A backup untested is a hope
lessons.html:
This module covers the survival layer: what a backup contains, the two custodies and their schedules, the Download Backups page, restores and the drill, the before-change backup, the continuity runbook beyond data, and the HealthTrade rehearsal.

The stakes, stated flat. The site holds the books, the stock ledger, the customer relationships, the tax evidence — the business's memory. Hardware fails, mistakes at scale happen (the import gone wrong, the bulk edit misfired), and hostile events exist. Backups are the difference between an incident and an ending. Every other module of this track assumes this one works.

The law, stated first because everything serves it: a backup untested is a hope. A backup file that exists proves storage was consumed; only a restore proves the business can come back. The industry's standing tragedy is the business that backed up faithfully for years and discovered at the fire that the files were empty, partial, or unrestorable. The restore drill (Chapter 5) is therefore not an advanced topic — it is the module's centre, and the monthly calendar line module 1 already placed.

The two custodies. On the managed platform, backup runs in both custodies of module 1's map, and the sysadmin must know exactly what each holds:

• The host's custody (CloudERP.One): the scheduled platform backups — nightly database and file backups on the infrastructure, replicated off-site per the hosting agreement. The sysadmin does not operate these but must hold their terms in writing: frequency, retention, off-site arrangement, and the two recovery numbers of Chapter 2.
• The site's custody (this certification): the periodic downloaded copy kept outside the platform entirely (Chapter 3's procedure), the before-change backup preceding every risky operation (Chapter 6), and the restore verification that tests the whole chain (Chapter 5).

Two custodies because each covers the other's failure mode: the host's machinery covers the site's daily risks at professional grade; the site's own off-platform copy covers the un-thinkable — the platform relationship itself failing, the account dispute, the regional event. A business whose only backups live inside the platform they back up has one custody, not two.

Module contents. Chapter 2: what a backup contains, and the two recovery numbers. Chapter 3: the Download Backups page and the off-platform copy. Chapter 4: restore paths on a managed platform. Chapter 5: the restore drill. Chapter 6: the before-change backup. Chapter 7: the continuity runbook. Chapter 8: the HealthTrade rehearsal. Chapter 9: review and the law.

lessons.title: Chapter 2 — What a backup contains, and the two numbers
lessons.html:
The anatomy. A complete site backup is two things, and the distinction is this chapter's most practical fact:

1. The database — every document, master, setting, permission, and log: the structured memory. This is the file most people mean by "the backup".
2. The files — the attachments: the invoice scans, the signed contracts, the voucher images, the product photos — stored as public and private file archives separate from the database dump.

A database-only backup restores a system whose every attachment link is broken — and since this programme attaches evidence to entries as standard practice (remittance returns, import approvals, count sheets), the files are part of the books. The completeness rule: a backup is database plus files, always, in both custodies. Chapter 8 shows HealthTrade learning this the cheap way.

What is not in the site backup. The apps (code) and platform configuration live in the host's custody and update stream — after a restore, the host re-provisions the site on current platform code with the restored data. This is why version notes matter in the backup log: data from a much older app version restores with a migration step the host performs.

The two recovery numbers — held in writing. The hosting agreement's continuity terms compress into two numbers the sysadmin must be able to quote:

• RPO — recovery point objective: how much recent work can be lost. Nightly backups mean an RPO of up to twenty-four hours: a failure at 5pm can lose the day. The business decides — as a policy, with the owner — whether that is acceptable for its trade; where it is not, the answer is raising backup frequency with the host, not hoping.
• RTO — recovery time objective: how long a restore takes end to end — from decision to a working site. The number shapes Chapter 7's runbook: an RTO of hours means the degraded-operation procedures must carry hours, not minutes.

Both numbers are confirmed with the host, written on the continuity page, and re-confirmed at the annual review — because the numbers people assume are always better than the numbers the agreement states, and the gap is discovered at the worst possible moment.

Practical rule: the monthly backup verification (Chapter 5) checks three completeness facts before anything else: the database file present, both file archives present, and the dates matching the schedule. Presence is the cheap check; the restore is the real one.

lessons.title: Chapter 3 — The Download Backups page and the off-platform copy
lessons.html:
Open Download Backups (awesome bar). This page is the site's own window on its backups: the recent backup sets listed with timestamps, each set offering its database download and its files downloads, plus the on-demand trigger to generate a fresh backup now. Two of this module's procedures run from this page.

Procedure one — the daily presence check (module 1's calendar line). Open the page; confirm yesterday's set exists with a plausible size and today's schedule ran. Thirty seconds. A missing or shrunken backup is raised the same day with the five-item report — this is the check that catches the silently-dead schedule before the month that needed it.

Procedure two — the off-platform copy (monthly, after the restore drill).

1. Trigger a fresh on-demand backup (or take the latest nightly set).
2. Download all components — the database file and both file archives. The database-only download habit is this module's classic quiet failure.
3. Store the set outside the platform: the business's own encrypted storage — a cloud drive under the business's account, plus, where the policy wants it, an offline copy. The point of this copy is surviving events that include the platform, so it cannot live on the platform.
4. Verify the copy: sizes match, the archive opens, the set is complete.
5. Log it: date, set timestamp, components, where stored, verified by whom.
6. Retention per the written policy — typically a rolling set of monthly copies plus the year-end copies kept long-term with the audit file. The retention line is written on the continuity page beside the recovery numbers, so the question of how far back the business can reach has one answer in one place.

Custody of the copies. The downloaded backup is the entire business in a file — every customer, every price, every salary. It is protected like the crown jewels it is:

• Stored encrypted, in storage the business controls (not a personal drive that leaves when a person does — the leaver procedure cannot chase personal storage).
• Access limited to the sysadmin and backstop, listed on the continuity page.
• Old copies beyond retention are properly destroyed, not abandoned on forgotten drives.

Practical rule: the off-platform copy is scheduled after the monthly restore drill on the calendar, so what goes off-platform each month is a set whose sibling was just proven restorable — the copy inherits the drill's confidence.

lessons.title: Chapter 4 — Restore paths on a managed platform
lessons.html:
Restores on a managed platform run through defined paths, and the sysadmin's competence is knowing which path fits which event before the event.

Path one — the full restore (the host performs it). The site is lost or corrupted beyond repair: the restore is a support request of the highest severity — the five-item report plus three restore-specific facts: which backup set (the timestamp, chosen deliberately: the last set before the damaging event, which is not always the latest set), restore where (over the live site, or to a parallel site for inspection first — the cautious default when time allows), and the authorisation (a full restore discards everything after the restore point; the decision is the owner's, on the record, because the restore's cost is the RPO made real: the work since the set is re-entered from the paper trail).

Path two — the test-site restore (the drill's path, Chapter 5). The same mechanics pointed at the test environment: a backup set restored to the test site, where it can be opened and read without touching production. This path is exercised monthly, which means the people, the request format, and the timing are all rehearsed when path one is suddenly needed — the drill is a fire drill precisely because it uses the real stairs.

Path three — the surgical recovery (restore-to-read). The most common real-world case is not a lost site but a damaged slice: the import that mangled a register, the bulk edit that overwrote a field, the cancellation cascade. A full restore would sacrifice everything since the set to fix one register — the wrong trade. The surgical path:

1. Restore the pre-event backup to the test site (path two's mechanics).
2. Read the damaged slice from the test site — the correct values, exported.
3. Repair production forward: a governed Update-type Data Import (module 3's procedure) or documented corrections, applying the correct values as a new, logged change.
4. Production's history stays intact — the damage and the repair both on the record, which is this programme's correction philosophy applied at scale.

Choosing the path — the three questions. What is damaged (everything, or a slice)? When was the last good state (which set)? What would a full restore cost (everything since the set — is the slice worth it)? The answers route the event; the runbook (Chapter 7) has them pre-printed.

Practical rule: in any restore conversation, name the backup set by timestamp in writing before anything runs. "Restore the backup" has destroyed more data than it has recovered; "restore the 03:12 set from the 14th, to the test site" is a procedure.

lessons.title: Chapter 5 — The restore drill
lessons.html:
The module's centre. The drill converts backup files into proven recoverability, monthly, on the calendar.

The monthly drill, as a procedure.

1. Pick this month's set — vary it: sometimes the latest nightly, sometimes the off-platform copy from storage (the copy must prove itself too, or it is decoration).
2. Restore to the test site — path two. On the managed platform this is the standing arrangement with the host or the self-service test-site mechanism, whichever the agreement provides; the drill also keeps that arrangement itself exercised.
3. Open and read. Presence is not the test — readability is: log in; open the Trial Balance and compare a known figure; open a recent Sales Invoice and its attachment (the files archive proving itself); run one report; check the restored set's document count against production's for the same date.
4. Time it. The end-to-end minutes are the site's real RTO evidence — trended, and compared against the number on the continuity page. A drifting drill time is a finding.
5. Sign it. One log line: date, set, path, checks passed, minutes, by whom. Twelve lines a year; the auditor's favourite page in this module.

What the drill catches — each one a real failure mode found cheap: the empty or truncated dump (storage consumed, nothing inside); the missing files archive (the database-only habit); the schedule that died silently weeks ago; the off-platform copy that never verified; the restore arrangement that changed at the host's end without the runbook noticing; and the RTO drifting from the promised number.

The annual full dress. Once a year the drill scales to the continuity rehearsal: the restore run as if real — the runbook followed literally from its first line, the communications step actually drafted, the degraded-operation procedures walked at one branch (the paper fallback from the POS track's till procedures), and the re-entry of a simulated gap rehearsed from the paper trail. The full dress is scheduled, announced, and reviewed — its findings amend the runbook, which is the point.

The psychology, stated once. Drills feel like waste precisely until they are survival, and the pressure to skip "just this month" arrives the first busy quarter. The counter is structural: the drill is a calendar line with an owner and an artifact, and a skipped drill is logged as skipped — visible in the twelve-line page. Two consecutive skips are an incident by policy.

Practical rule: the first drill ever run at a site is the most valuable single hour in this track — it converts every assumption on the continuity page into either evidence or a finding. Run it in week one of taking the role, not month one.

lessons.title: Chapter 6 — The before-change backup
lessons.html:
Backups defend against two event families: the catastrophic (rare) and the self-inflicted (regular). This chapter is the second family's discipline: the on-demand backup as the standing precondition for risky operations.

The rule. Before any operation that changes data or structure at scale, a fresh on-demand backup is taken from the Download Backups page and its timestamp is written into the operation's log line — backup 14:22 taken; import run 14:31. The operations that qualify:

• Every Data Import beyond trivial size (module 3's step 4 — this chapter is where it comes from).
• Every bulk edit or bulk rename/merge batch.
• Every customisation deployment and settings change with data reach (module 5's change procedure includes this line).
• Every update window the host announces (the host backs up too; the site's own set is the belt to their braces).
• Anything the sysadmin hesitates over. Hesitation is the trigger; the backup costs one minute.

Why the timestamp matters. The before-change backup's whole value is being the last set before the event — the exact restore point Chapter 4's surgical path needs. A recovery that has to choose between "the nightly from before, losing the morning's trade" and "the nightly from after, containing the damage" is a recovery the one-minute backup would have made trivial.

The paired habit — the operation log. The backup timestamp lives in the ops log line that every governed operation already writes (imports: module 3; changes: module 5; incidents: module 7). The pairing means any operation can be unwound with precision: the log names what ran and when; the timestamp names the recovery point; the surgical path does the rest. An operation with no log line and no backup is the definition of ungoverned — whatever it was.

The recovery decision, when a change goes wrong. The paths from Chapter 4, applied small:

1. Reversible in-system? The mis-imported records disabled or corrected by a counter-import; the bulk edit re-run with correct values. First choice — history stays whole.
2. Surgical restore-to-read? The before-change set to the test site; correct values read; production repaired forward. Second choice.
3. Full restore to the before-change set? Only when the damage is pervasive and the window since the backup is small — which, because the backup was taken immediately before, it usually is. This is the one scenario where full restore is routinely cheap: the window is minutes.

Practical rule: teach the rule as a reflex with one sentence — no backup timestamp in the log line, no run. It survives staff changes better than any paragraph.

lessons.title: Chapter 7 — The continuity runbook
lessons.html:
Backups recover data; continuity keeps the business operating while recovery happens. The runbook is one document, printed and stored where a dead site cannot take it, covering the four scenarios.

Scenario 1 — the site is down.

1. Confirm and scope (one user or all? the custody map's first question), note the exact time.
2. Raise with the host at incident severity — the five-item report; the runbook carries the support channel's details and the escalation path on paper.
3. Communicate inward: one message to staff from the sysadmin — what is known, what to do meanwhile, when the next update comes. Silence breeds improvisation; improvisation breeds the un-entered sale.
4. Degraded operation begins (scenario 4's procedures).
5. On restoration: the gap re-entered from the paper trail, the incident logged with timeline and cause.

Scenario 2 — data damage, site up. The import/bulk-edit family: Chapter 4's three questions, the surgical path as default, the before-change set as the anchor, the repair forward, the log.

Scenario 3 — the security event. A credential suspected compromised, a session that should not exist, an integration key exposed: the affected account disabled first and investigated second (disabling is reversible; the damage of waiting is not), passwords and keys rotated per module 8's procedures, the host informed where platform-side action is needed, and the event logged with its timeline. The runbook lists, on paper, who may order these steps.

Scenario 4 — degraded operation. The business trades through the outage:

• The tills: the paper fallback from the POS track — pre-printed sale slips, the count discipline unchanged, everything re-entered in order on restoration. The runbook states where the pads live and who owns the re-entry.
• Payments: the release rules do not relax because the system is down — the mandate and the separation hold on paper; anything that cannot be verified waits.
• The re-entry: owned, sequenced (documents re-entered in occurrence order with honest dates), and reconciled — the first post-restoration close pays extra attention to the gap days.

The people layer. The runbook's last page is names: the sysadmin, the backstop, the owner, the host's channel, the off-platform storage's location and access holders — with the standing rule that the backstop can execute every scenario alone, because incidents schedule themselves for leave days. Module 1's backstop design is load-bearing exactly here.

Keeping it live. The runbook is amended by every drill's findings and every real incident's lessons, re-printed on amendment, and walked in the annual full dress. A runbook last touched two years ago is a museum piece describing a system that no longer exists.

lessons.title: Chapter 8 — Case study: HealthTrade's continuity year
lessons.html:
The survival layer, installed and tested. Every chapter appears.

The ground. Module 1's audit line — an untested backup — unpacks into the standard findings: the host's nightly backups running faithfully (confirmed in writing: nightly, thirty-day retention, off-site replication; RPO twenty-four hours, RTO stated in hours); no site-side copy anywhere; no drill ever; no runbook; and the previous "backup habit" — an occasional database download by the old implementation partner — database-only, no files archives, ever.

Week one — the first drill. Run per Chapter 5's advice in the first week of the role. The latest nightly set restores to the test site; the Trial Balance matches; the document counts agree — and check 3's attachment test fails on the partner's old downloads: the database-only habit is exposed on the spot as a restore that opens invoices whose evidence is gone. Finding logged; the completeness rule (database plus both files archives) written into the procedure; the drill signed at forty minutes end to end. The continuity page gets its first honest numbers.

Month one — the custodies established. The off-platform copy procedure starts: full set downloaded after the drill, stored encrypted in business-controlled storage, access limited to the sysadmin and backstop, logged. The before-change rule is instituted with the reflex sentence — no backup timestamp in the log line, no run — and its first exercise arrives within weeks: module 3's price-list import runs with its 14:22 timestamp on record.

Month three — the rule pays for itself. A supplier-record bulk edit misfires — a wrong field written across 136 suppliers. The response is Chapter 6's decision tree run calmly: reversible in-system? No — the old values are gone from production. Surgical path: the before-change set (taken eleven minutes earlier) restores to the test site; the correct field values export; a governed Update-type import repairs production forward; total damage window, one hour of procurement queries; total data lost, zero. The incident log's closing line: the one-minute backup bought back the afternoon.

Month six — the full dress. The annual rehearsal runs early, announced: the runbook followed from line one for a simulated outage, the staff communication actually drafted and sent to a test list, the Ibadan tills trading ninety minutes on the paper pads with the count discipline holding, and the re-entry rehearsed in order the next morning. Findings: the runbook's paper copy was only at head office (branch copies printed), and one till had no pad (stocked). The runbook is amended, re-printed, and signed.

The year's page. Twelve drill lines, zero skips. Off-platform copies: twelve, all verified. Before-change backups: every logged operation carries its timestamp. One real recovery, surgical, zero loss. The MD's note: we used to hope; now we rehearse.

lessons.title: Chapter 9 — Common mistakes & the fourth law
lessons.html:
The survival layer's recurring failures, then the review list.

Pattern 1 — the untested backup. Symptom: years of backup files, zero restores ever; confidence proportional to file count rather than evidence. Cause: presence mistaken for recoverability (Chapters 1, 5). Fix: the first drill this week, the monthly drill on the calendar with its signed line, and the skipped-drill-is-logged rule with two skips an incident.

Pattern 2 — the database-only habit. Symptom: downloads and copies that carry the dump and never the files archives; a restore that opens invoices whose attachments are gone — the books stripped of their evidence. Cause: "the backup" misunderstood as one file (Chapter 2). Fix: the completeness rule — database plus both files archives, always, in both custodies — and the drill's attachment check enforcing it monthly.

Pattern 3 — the single custody. Symptom: every backup living inside the platform it backs up; nothing the business itself holds. Cause: the host's competence mistaken for the whole design (Chapters 1, 3). Fix: the monthly off-platform copy — complete, encrypted, business-controlled, verified, logged — scheduled after the drill so it inherits proven restorability.

Pattern 4 — the assumed numbers. Symptom: nobody can quote the RPO or RTO; everyone assumes better than the agreement states; the gap surfaces mid-incident. Cause: the recovery numbers never confirmed in writing (Chapter 2). Fix: both numbers on the continuity page, confirmed with the host, re-confirmed annually, and tested against the drill's timings.

Pattern 5 — the unlogged operation. Symptom: a damaged register and no before-change set; the recovery forced to choose between losing the morning and keeping the damage. Cause: the before-change rule absent or skipped under pressure (Chapter 6). Fix: the reflex sentence — no backup timestamp in the log line, no run — enforced by the ops-log pairing and audited in the monthly import-log reconciliation.

Pattern 6 — the museum runbook. Symptom: a continuity document nobody has opened in years, naming departed people and dead channels; the incident improvised around it. Cause: the runbook written once and never exercised (Chapter 7). Fix: amendment after every drill and incident, the annual full dress walking it literally, branch paper copies current, and the backstop able to execute every scenario alone.

The review list. Before the quiz, confirm you can: state the two custodies and what each covers; name a backup's two components and why files are part of the books; quote and source the RPO and RTO; run the daily presence check and the monthly off-platform copy from the Download Backups page with its custody rules; choose among the three restore paths with the three questions, and name sets by timestamp; run the monthly drill's five steps and the annual full dress; apply the before-change rule and its decision tree; and walk the runbook's four scenarios including degraded tills and governed re-entry.

The fourth law: a backup untested is a hope — copies in two custodies, complete to the file, restores rehearsed monthly, and continuity written where a dead site cannot take it. Module 5 covers updates, changes, and the test discipline.

changes_updates.title: Sysadmin 5 — Updates, Changes & the Test Discipline
changes_updates.desc: Updates and change control in ZhiftERP: the staged/documented/reversible discipline across the host's update stream and the site's customisations; the test site with its refresh rhythm and identity rules; the layer ladder from Customize Form through Custom Fields to scripts with the lowest-layer rule; the five-part customisation register and its annual reconciliation; the eight-step change procedure scaled by weight; and the twelve-minute smoke test with its amendment rule.

lessons.title: Chapter 1 — Every change is staged, documented, reversible
lessons.html:
This module covers changes to the system itself: platform updates from the host's stream, the test environment, the customisation layers from Customize Form to code, the customisation register, the change procedure, and the smoke test.

Why change is its own module. Every other module governs data inside a stable system. This one governs changes to the system — new versions, new fields, changed forms, new logic. Change is where stable systems break, and the breakage has a signature: it lands on the busiest doctype, at the busiest hour, and its cause is whatever nobody wrote down. The discipline is three words, and every chapter serves them:

• Staged — every change runs in the test environment before it runs in production. No exceptions for "small" changes: the field relabel that hides a mandatory field breaks posting exactly as thoroughly as a code change.
• Documented — every change has a register entry: what, why, who owns it, when, and the test evidence. Chapter 5's register is the module's central artifact.
• Reversible — every change deploys behind a before-change backup (module 4's rule, applied to structure as well as data) and with its undo path named in advance.

The two change streams.

1. The host's stream — updates. CloudERP.One updates the platform and the apps: security patches, fixes, version upgrades. The sysadmin does not write these but receives them governed: release notes read, the test site updated first, the smoke test run, the window scheduled. Chapter 2.
2. The site's stream — customisations. The business's own changes: form adjustments, custom fields, notifications, workflows, and — governed hardest — scripts. Chapters 3-5.

The standing tension, named honestly. The business wants changes fast; the discipline adds a day. The answer is not to argue the discipline down but to make its fast lane genuinely fast: a Customize Form change staged, signed, and deployed inside one day is the standard this module builds — slow governance breeds cowboy changes exactly as module 3's slow request lane breeds duplicate masters.

Module contents. Chapter 2: the host's update stream, received governed. Chapter 3: the test environment. Chapter 4: the customisation layers — Customize Form, Custom Fields, and code. Chapter 5: the customisation register. Chapter 6: the change procedure end to end. Chapter 7: the smoke test. Chapter 8: the HealthTrade case. Chapter 9: review and the law.

lessons.title: Chapter 2 — The update stream, received governed
lessons.html:
The host maintains the platform: security patches, bug fixes, and version upgrades arrive on CloudERP.One's schedule. The sysadmin's job is receiving them so the site never learns by surprise.

The update kinds, by weight.

• Security patches — applied promptly by the host, sometimes without a scheduling conversation; the sysadmin's job is the after-check (the smoke test's short form) and staying informed.
• Maintenance releases — fixes within the current version; low risk, still received governed: notes read, test first where the window allows.
• Version upgrades — the heavy events: new major versions change behaviour, layouts, and occasionally the ground under customisations. These are scheduled like the projects they are.

The receiving procedure.

1. Read the release notes against the site. The host announces what changes; the sysadmin reads with the module map open (module 1) and the customisation register beside it (Chapter 5): which of our modules are touched, which of our customisations sit on ground that is moving. Ten minutes that convert an announcement into an impact list.
2. Update the test site first. The standing arrangement with the host: the test environment receives the update ahead of production. The smoke test (Chapter 7) runs there, plus targeted checks on the impact list.
3. Schedule the production window. Off-peak for the business — never the close week, never month-end filing days; the calendar (module 1) marks the standing no-update windows. Staff are told: when, how long, what to expect.
4. The before-change backup — the site's own on-demand set, timestamped in the log, belt to the host's braces (module 4's rule).
5. The update runs (the host's hands), then the smoke test runs (the sysadmin's). Chapter 7's checklist, immediately, before staff resume — findings raised on the spot while the window is still open.
6. Log and announce. The version change recorded (the About page's new numbers into the register), the all-clear sent, anything user-visible noted in one line.

The deferral question. Can updates be postponed? Maintenance and features, within reason and by agreement. Security patches, no — a known vulnerability on a system holding the books is not a scheduling preference. The written update policy states both halves so the conversation never happens under pressure.

Practical rule: the update that has never caused a problem is the one that breeds the skipped smoke test — and the skipped smoke test is how the print-format break trades quietly for three days until a customer receives a broken invoice. Run the checklist every time; it is twelve minutes.

lessons.title: Chapter 3 — The test environment
lessons.html:
The test site is the module's load-bearing infrastructure: a second site, provisioned by the host, that exists to absorb risk production must never see.

What runs there — the standing list.

• Restore drills (module 4's monthly line — the drill and this chapter share the site).
• Update previews (Chapter 2's step 2).
• Customisation builds and sign-offs (Chapters 4-6): every change is built here, and the requesting owner approves it here, on realistic data, before production hears of it.
• Import slices (module 3's ten-row dry runs).
• Training and experiments: the new cashier's practice sessions, the "what happens if" questions — answered here where the answer costs nothing.

The refresh cycle. A test site drifts from production — data ages, settings diverge — and a stale test site gives stale answers: the customisation that worked in test against last year's data meets this year's volumes differently. The procedure: refresh the test site from a production backup on a schedule (monthly rides naturally on the restore drill — the drill's restore is the refresh) and always before a heavy piece of work (a version-upgrade preview, a big import rehearsal). The refresh is logged like the backups it comes from.

The two rules that keep the test site honest.

1. Test data discipline. The refreshed test site contains real business data — the same customers, salaries, and prices as production — so it is protected by the same access design: module 2's permissions apply, test-site accounts are real named accounts, and the leaver procedure covers both sites. A test site with an open door is a production data breach with extra steps.
2. Unmistakable identity. The test site must announce itself — the site name distinct, and where the platform supports it, a visual banner — because the standing accident is the document entered into the wrong site: the real invoice typed into test (lost work) or the test experiment typed into production (a correction case). Every training session opens by pointing at the identity markers.

What test does not prove. Honest limits, stated once: the test site proves function, not scale (production's concurrent load and full history behave differently at the margins), and proves the change, not the users (the front line will find the path no tester walked). The smoke test after production deployment (Chapter 7) exists because test passing is necessary, never sufficient.

Practical rule: the test site's health is a monthly calendar line — reachable, refreshed on schedule, access list current. A dead test site quietly converts every future change into test-in-production, which is Chapter 9's first pattern.

lessons.title: Chapter 4 — The customisation layers
lessons.html:
Site customisations come in layers, ordered by power and therefore by governance weight. The standing rule: solve at the lowest layer that solves it.

Layer 1 — Customize Form. Open Customize Form (awesome bar), select the doctype, and adjust its presentation and behaviour without code:

• Relabel fields to the business's language; reorder; hide fields the business never uses (a hidden field simplifies every day at that keyboard).
• Set fields mandatory (module 3's completeness enforcement lives here), set defaults, set read-only.
• Adjust list settings and search fields.

Customize Form changes are stored as overrides on top of the standard doctype — they survive updates and can be reverted per property. This is the workhorse layer: most business requests ("can this field be required", "can we hide that section") end here, and its fast lane should run inside a day. Two cautions carry its whole risk: hiding or requiring a field affects every role that touches the form (impact analysis is still real), and mandatory-with-history means old incomplete records now block on edit — decided knowingly.

Layer 2 — Custom Fields. Adding fields the business needs that the standard form lacks — the delivery route on an invoice, the licence number on a customer. Created through Customize Form (or the Custom Field doctype directly), with the discipline:

• Named to be recognisable as custom (the platform prefixes internally; the label and description state the business meaning).
• Typed correctly at birth — a Link to a proper master beats free text every time it will be filtered or reported on (a free-text "route" field yields seventeen spellings of one route; a Link to a Route master yields a report).
• Positioned deliberately in the form's flow, and added to list/print views where it earns it.
• Registered — every custom field is a register entry (Chapter 5) with an owner and a purpose. The field nobody can explain is this module's version of the account nobody can explain.

Custom fields survive updates; their meaning is what decays without the register.

Layer 3 — logic: Notifications, Workflows, and scripts. Notifications (module 6) and Workflows (module 2) are configuration-level logic — governed, but codeless. Client and Server Scripts are the code layer: real programming inside the site, capable of anything and therefore governed hardest — specified in writing, built and tested in the test site, reviewed, registered with an owner, and — the platform reality — server-side code on managed hosting may be restricted or routed through the host's review, which is a feature: the constraint is the governance. The rule that keeps this layer small: a script is the last resort after Customize Form, a custom field, a Notification, and a Workflow have each been ruled out in writing.

lessons.title: Chapter 5 — The customisation register
lessons.html:
The register is one page per customisation, and the collection is the site's memory of how it differs from standard. It is the module's central artifact because every other discipline depends on it: update impact analysis reads it, the change procedure writes it, and the annual reconciliation proves it.

The entry, per customisation.

1. What — the object, precisely: the doctype, the field/property/script name, the layer (Customize Form / Custom Field / Notification / Workflow / Script).
2. Why — the business purpose in one sentence, in the owner's words. This line is the one that saves the next sysadmin.
3. Who — the requesting owner (the person who answers "do we still need this") and the builder.
4. When — requested, tested, deployed — with the test sign-off and the before-change backup timestamp.
5. The undo path — how this comes out cleanly if retired: revert the property, hide-don't-delete the field (a custom field with data is retired by hiding, never deleting — the data is history), disable the notification, version the script.

Why the register earns its keep, three ways.

• Update safety: Chapter 2's step 1 reads release notes against the register — "the invoice form is changing in this version; we have three customisations on it" is a sentence only a register can produce.
• The explanation debt: without the register, every field accumulates the question "what does this do, who wanted it, can we remove it" — and the safe answer to unexplained structure is always "leave it", which is how sites fossilise. With the register, retirement is routine.
• Continuity: the register is the customisation chapter of module 4's handover — a new sysadmin reads it and knows the site.

The annual reconciliation. Once a year (the calendar's customisation line): the site's actual customisations are listed from the system's own records — the Customize Form overrides, the Custom Field list, the Notification and Workflow lists, the script list — and reconciled against the register. Three findings and their handling:

1. On the site, not in the register — the undocumented change: registered retroactively with its archaeology, and the gap in the change procedure that admitted it is fixed.
2. In the register, not on the site — the ghost entry: closed with a note.
3. Registered but unowned — the owner left; the entry is re-homed or the customisation is nominated for retirement at the owner review: each owner re-confirms annually that their customisations still earn their place. Sites accrete; the review is the pruning.

Practical rule: the register's quality test is the stranger test — could a competent stranger, given only the register, explain every difference between this site and a standard install? Module 4's handover test, applied to structure.

lessons.title: Chapter 6 — The change procedure, end to end
lessons.html:
One procedure covers every site-stream change, scaled by weight. Eight steps; the light version runs inside a day.

1. The request, written. Who wants it, what outcome, why — in the requester's words. "Add a field" is not a request; "we need to record the delivery route on invoices so dispatch can plan" is. The outcome framing matters because step 2 may find a lower-layer answer than the requester imagined.

2. Impact analysis, with the maps. The module map (who works in this doctype), the register (what already customises it), and the layer question (Chapter 4's lowest-layer rule). Output: the chosen layer, the affected roles and prints and reports, and the undo path — three sentences for a small change, a page for a script.

3. Build in test. On the refreshed test site, never production. For Customize Form work this is minutes; the discipline is the venue, not the effort.

4. Owner sign-off in test. The requesting owner exercises the change on the test site against realistic data and approves in writing (a message suffices; it goes in the register entry). This step kills the commonest failure — the change that technically matches the request and practically misses the need — while it is still free.

5. The before-change backup. Module 4's rule: the on-demand set, timestamp into the log line. For structure changes as for data.

6. Deploy, in a sane window. Small changes: any quiet moment, announced where user-visible. Anything touching posting paths or many roles: the same off-peak discipline as updates. Never the close week.

7. Verify live. The smoke test's targeted form: the changed path exercised in production immediately — the field appears, the mandatory enforces, the notification fires — plus one standard document through the touched doctype (the posting map check where posting is anywhere near the change).

8. Register and announce. The register entry completed (Chapter 5's five parts), and the one-line announcement to the affected roles: what changed, what it looks like, who to tell if something is off. An unannounced change generates a week of "is this broken?" tickets that one sentence prevents.

Scaling by weight. The steps never drop; their depth scales. A relabel: steps 1-2 are two sentences, 3-4 ten minutes, the whole lane a morning. A script: every step is real work and the timeline is honest about it. What never happens at any weight: skipping test ("it's tiny"), skipping the owner ("it's obvious"), skipping the register ("I'll remember") — Chapter 9's patterns are exactly these three skips, aged.

Practical rule: pre-print the eight steps as the change ticket's template. A procedure that lives in the ticket gets followed; one that lives in a manual gets remembered selectively.

lessons.title: Chapter 7 — The smoke test
lessons.html:
After every update and every significant deployment, the smoke test proves the site's critical paths before staff resume. It is a written checklist, owned, timed at roughly twelve minutes, and its logic is the posting map exercised live.

The standing checklist.

1. Login and Desk — a standard (non-admin) account logs in; the workspaces render; the awesome bar answers.
2. The trading path — one test Sales Invoice: created, submitted, View > Accounting Ledger read (the rows match the posting map), printed to PDF (the print path proves the format and letterhead survived — the classic silent casualty of updates), then cancelled clean.
3. The stock path — one Stock Entry or Delivery Note cycle where stock is live: submit, ledger read, cancel.
4. The payment path — one Payment Entry against the test invoice before its cancellation: references resolve, the bank leaf posts.
5. The reports — the Trial Balance and one standard report per live module open and render with plausible figures.
6. The channels — one email sends from the site and arrives (the queue moves — module 6); one Notification fires where quickly testable.
7. The customisation spot-checks — from the register: the custom fields visible, the key Customize Form properties holding (the mandatory still mandatory), any script's happy path exercised. The register makes this step a list, not a memory exercise.
8. The integrations — each registered integration's health check (module 6's register defines it; for the e-invoicing rail, the check the tax module relies on).

The rules around it.

• Run before staff resume, inside the window — a finding raised while the host's hands are still on the update is a fix; the same finding on Thursday is an incident with three days of consequences.
• Documents are test-marked and cleaned: the test invoice is cancelled, the test entries reversed — the smoke test must not leave droppings in the books (use the standing test customer/item so even the residue is recognisable).
• Log the run: date, trigger (which update/change), checks passed, minutes, by whom — one line beside the update's register entry. Findings get the incident treatment: logged, raised or fixed, and — where the smoke test itself missed something that surfaced later — the checklist is amended, which is how the list earns its shape over the years.

Practical rule: the smoke test is deliberately shallow and wide — every critical path touched once, nothing exhaustively. Depth belongs in the test site before deployment; the smoke test only proves the deployment landed. Twelve minutes, every time, no exceptions for boring updates: the boring update that breaks printing is this module's oldest story.

lessons.title: Chapter 8 — Case study: HealthTrade's change year
lessons.html:
The change discipline, installed and exercised. Every chapter appears.

The ground. The site carries the implementation era's accumulation: customisations nobody listed, a test site that exists but was last refreshed "sometime last year", and update history in the host's records only. The first annual reconciliation (Chapter 5) is run retroactively: the site's actual overrides, custom fields, notifications, and workflows are listed from the system's own records — 14 customisations found, of which 9 are explained and registered with owners, and 5 defy explanation. The five get the archaeology: two turn out to be abandoned experiments (retired — the custom fields hidden, not deleted, per the undo rule), one is a duplicate of standard behaviour (retired), and two are quietly load-bearing (registered with their reconstructed purpose and new owners). The register exists by month's end; the stranger test passes.

The test site brought honest. The refresh cycle is tied to the restore drill (module 4's monthly restore is the refresh), the identity banner is confirmed unmistakable after one near-miss in training week (a practice invoice nearly typed into production — the trainer's story becomes the standing example), and the access list is aligned with module 2's matrix.

A change through the lane (Chapters 4, 6). Dispatch requests delivery-route tracking on invoices. The lane runs as designed: the written request names the outcome; impact analysis chooses Layer 2 — a custom Route master (a tiny doctype) and a Link field on the Sales Invoice, explicitly rejecting the free-text shortcut ("seventeen spellings of one route yields no report"); built in test in an afternoon; the dispatch owner signs off in test after one adjustment (the field moved next to the shipping address, where the eye goes); before-change backup at 07:14; deployed in the morning quiet; verified live (field present, link resolves, one test invoice through the posting map); registered; announced in one line. Elapsed: two working days, most of it the owner's sign-off latency. The fast lane earns its reputation, and the next three requests arrive through the lane rather than around it.

An update cycle (Chapters 2, 7). The host announces a maintenance release. The notes are read against the register (one touched area: printing). The test site updates first; the targeted check passes there — but the production smoke test's step 2 catches it anyway: the invoice PDF renders with the letterhead displaced. Raised inside the window with the exact reproduction; the host applies the fix before staff resume; the smoke-test log's line reads finding raised and closed in-window. The checklist's print step, already the list's veteran, keeps its seat. The MD's note for the quarter: the system now changes the way the books close — on a procedure, with evidence, and nothing by surprise.

lessons.title: Chapter 9 — Common mistakes & the fifth law
lessons.html:
The change layer's recurring failures, then the review list.

Pattern 1 — test-in-production. Symptom: experiments run live; "let's just try it" on the real books; the correction traffic that follows. Cause: no test site, or a dead one (Chapter 3). Fix: the test site as standing infrastructure — refreshed on the drill's rhythm, identity unmistakable, health on the calendar — and the venue rule absolute: every change builds in test, at every weight.

Pattern 2 — the undocumented site. Symptom: fields nobody can explain; the "what does this do" question answered with "leave it"; a site that fossilises because removal is riskier than accretion. Cause: changes without register entries (Chapter 5). Fix: the retroactive reconciliation once — archaeology, ownership, retirements — then the register as step 8 of every change, and the annual owner review pruning what no longer earns its place.

Pattern 3 — the surprise update. Symptom: the platform changes and the business discovers it from breakage; printing dies on a Tuesday; nobody read the notes. Cause: the host's stream received ungoverned (Chapter 2). Fix: the receiving procedure — notes against the register, test first, scheduled window, before-change backup, smoke test before staff resume — and the update policy's written line on what may be deferred and what may not.

Pattern 4 — the script reflex. Symptom: code as the first answer; a thicket of scripts doing what Customize Form, a custom field, a Notification, or a Workflow would do; every update a minefield. Cause: the lowest-layer rule unknown or unenforced (Chapter 4). Fix: the layer ladder applied in writing at impact analysis, the script bar set high (last resort, specified, reviewed, owned), and the thicket thinned at the annual review.

Pattern 5 — the skipped smoke test. Symptom: "the update was boring" — and the break trades quietly for days until a customer or the close finds it. Cause: the checklist treated as optional for routine events (Chapter 7). Fix: the twelve minutes every time, the run logged beside the update entry, and the checklist amended by every miss so it compounds instead of decaying.

Pattern 6 — the free-text field. Symptom: a custom field filled seventeen ways; reports impossible; the cleanup import annual. Cause: typed wrong at birth (Chapter 4). Fix: the Link-to-master discipline for anything that will be filtered or reported, and the retype done once, properly — a small master, a governed migration of values, the register entry updated.

The review list. Before the quiz, confirm you can: state the three-word discipline and the two change streams; run the update receiving procedure including the deferral policy's two halves; keep the test site honest — refresh rhythm, data discipline, unmistakable identity — and state what test does not prove; walk the layer ladder from Customize Form through Custom Fields to scripts with the lowest-layer rule; write a five-part register entry and run the annual reconciliation's three findings; execute the eight-step change procedure scaled by weight; and run the smoke test's eight checks with its rules.

The fifth law: every change is staged in test, signed by its owner, deployed behind a backup, verified live, and written in the register — the site never learns by surprise. Module 6 covers the channels: printing, email, and integrations.

email_integrations.title: Sysadmin 6 — Printing, Email & Integrations
email_integrations.desc: Channels in ZhiftERP: the channel rule and inventory; Letter Head and Print Settings with the specimen discipline; Print Formats by the three levels with nothing hard-typed; the domain sending identity on the Email Account record with the identity test; the Email Queue's daily glance, stuck-queue procedure, and volume read; scoped Notifications and Auto Email Reports with the annual review; and integration governance — dedicated users, credential custody, the register with health checks, and the quarterly door count, with the NGE Portal e-invoicing rail as the standing example.

lessons.title: Chapter 1 — The channels: every one owned
lessons.html:
This module covers the system's faces to the world: printed documents, email, and integrations. Each is a channel — a path by which the system speaks or connects — and the module's design is one rule applied three ways: every channel has an owner, an identity the business controls, credentials under custody, and a health read on the calendar.

Why channels get a module. Channels fail differently from data. A data error is wrong inside the system, found by the system's own checks. A channel failure is silence or embarrassment outside the system:

• The email queue stalls, and the statements Process Statement Of Accounts faithfully generated arrive nowhere — collections weakens for a month before anyone connects the dots.
• The invoice prints with a stretched logo and a missing tax line — every customer receives the business's carelessness in PDF form.
• The e-invoicing integration's credential expires, and the compliance rail the tax module depends on goes quiet.

None of these announce themselves in a list view. The module's machinery — the queue read, the print standards, the integration register with its health checks — exists to make channel failures loud and fast instead of quiet and slow.

The channel inventory. The sysadmin keeps one page listing every channel:

1. Print — the document formats and the letterhead (Chapters 2-3).
2. Email out — the sending identity, the queue, the automated senders: Notifications, Auto Email Reports, the statement run (Chapters 4-6).
3. Email in — where inbound mail creates or updates records, where configured.
4. Integrations — every external system connected: the e-invoicing rail (NGE Portal), payment or SMS gateways where used, and anything with an API key (Chapters 7-8).

Per channel: the owner, the identity (domain, sender address, credential), where the credential lives, the health check, and the known failure mode. This inventory is the module's register, and module 1's monthly integration line reads from it — a channel missing from the inventory is a channel whose failure will be diagnosed from zero, at the worst time.

Module contents. Chapter 2: Letter Head and Print Settings. Chapter 3: Print Formats. Chapter 4: Email Accounts — the sending identity. Chapter 5: the Email Queue. Chapter 6: Notifications and Auto Email Reports. Chapter 7: integrations and credential custody. Chapter 8: the integration register and the HealthTrade case. Chapter 9: review and the law.

lessons.title: Chapter 2 — Letter Head and Print Settings
lessons.html:
Every printed document carries the business's face before it carries its figures. Two doctypes set the standard once.

The Letter Head doctype. Open Letter Head (awesome bar): the header (and optionally footer) that rides every printed document — the logo, the legal name, addresses, registration and tax identifiers, contacts. The rules:

• Content is a policy decision, not a design whim: what must legally appear on an invoice (registration numbers, tax identity) is confirmed with the accountant; the letterhead is where it lives once so no format forgets it.
• One default, marked: the default letterhead applies everywhere automatically; additional letterheads exist only for real cases (a second company on the site gets its own — the multi-company rule reaching into print; a branch variant only if genuinely needed).
• The image discipline: the logo uploaded at proper resolution, sized in the letterhead itself, and tested to PDF before the letterhead ships — the stretched-logo invoice is this chapter's classic failure, and it is a two-minute test.
• Changes are governed events: a letterhead change alters every document printed from that day — module 5's change lane applies (test site, sign-off, register), and old printed documents in circulation mean the change date is worth logging.

Print Settings. Open Print Settings: the site-wide print policy page, walked once like every settings page:

• The PDF page size (A4 for Nigerian business correspondence), fonts and text sizing where exposed.
• Letterhead-by-default on, so nothing prints naked.
• Currency and amount formatting confirmed against System Settings' precision decisions (module 1) — the amount that displays differently on screen and paper is a settings mismatch, not a bug.
• The print server / PDF generation options as provided by the platform, noted in the walk record.

The standing test. After any change to letterhead, print settings, or formats — and inside every smoke test (module 5's step 2) — one document of each critical kind is printed to PDF and read like a customer would: logo clean, identity complete, figures aligned, totals and tax lines present, footer intact. The PDF is the product here; the screen preview approximates it but the PDF is what leaves the building.

Practical rule: collect one signed-off specimen PDF per critical document (invoice, statement, receipt, purchase order) in the channel register. The specimen is the standard the smoke test compares against — "does it still look like this" is a faster and stricter test than "does it look right".

lessons.title: Chapter 3 — Print Formats
lessons.html:
The Print Format decides how each doctype renders on paper. The letterhead is the frame; the format is the body.

The three levels, by governance weight (module 5's layer ladder, applied to print).

1. The standard formats — every doctype ships with one. Adequate for internal documents; the default starting point.
2. The Print Format Builder — the codeless editor: open a doctype's print view, choose to customise, and arrange fields, columns, and sections by drag and configuration. This is the workhorse for business-facing documents: the invoice showing the fields this business's customers need (the custom Route field from module 5 earning its print placement here), columns ordered for readability, the remarks section where signatures go.
3. Custom HTML formats — code-level control for pixel-specific needs. Module 5's script rules apply verbatim: last resort, specified, tested in the test site, registered with an owner — and every platform update's smoke test exercises them, because code-level formats are the update's favourite casualty.

The assignment discipline. Each doctype has a default format; users with print access can often choose among available formats at print time. Governance:

• The default per critical doctype is a decision in the channel register — the invoice's default is the signed-off specimen's format, full stop.
• Redundant and draft formats are cleaned up or clearly named (DRAFT — do not use beats a menu of five plausible invoices).
• Where a real second format exists (a delivery-note variant without prices for drivers, a proforma), it is named for its purpose and listed in the register with its use case.

Format content rules, carried from the tracks. The programme's modules have already decided much of what must print; the sysadmin implements:

• The invoice: the tax lines and identifiers the tax module requires, the payment terms and bank details the receivables routine relies on (details from the system's master records — never typed into the format, where they fossilise).
• The statement: the format Process Statement Of Accounts sends — tested by sending one to a test address and reading it as the customer.
• The receipt and the POS print: the POS track's till formats, referenced here for completeness.

Practical rule: fields print from the document; identity prints from the letterhead; nothing prints from text hard-typed into a format. The hard-typed bank account that survived three real account changes is a known way businesses direct customer payments to a closed account — the channel register's specimen review catches it.

lessons.title: Chapter 4 — Email Accounts: the sending identity
lessons.html:
Open Email Account (awesome bar). Every email the site sends or receives runs through an Email Account record, and the identity question is settled here.

The outgoing account. The record carries the sender address, the mail service's connection settings (as the platform and the business's mail provider require), and the flags that matter:

• Enable Outgoing — this account may send.
• Default Outgoing — the site's standing sender: transaction emails, statements, notifications all leave under this identity unless a specific account overrides.

The identity rule — the chapter's core. The sending address is an address at the business's own domain (accounts@ the business's domain), never a personal mailbox and never a free-mail address. Three reasons, each sufficient:

1. Deliverability: business mail systems increasingly distrust free-mail senders for commercial documents; the domain identity with the provider's proper authentication is what lands statements in inboxes rather than spam folders. The deliverability setup (the domain's mail authentication records) is done once with the domain's custodian — the difference between the statement run working and silently decorating spam folders.
2. Continuity: a personal mailbox leaves with its person — the leaver procedure cannot chase it, and the sent history goes with them.
3. Identity: the customer's reply, the dispute, the audit trail — all anchored to an address the business controls.

The credential custody. The mail account's password/app-credential is an integration credential (Chapter 7's rules apply): held in the business's credential custody, not in one person's head; rotated on the security calendar and at relevant leavers; and — the operational note that saves a future incident — rotation includes updating the Email Account record, because the rotated password that never reached the site is the stuck-queue incident of Chapter 5 waiting to happen.

Incoming accounts, where used. An Email Account can also receive — Enable Incoming — and file inbound mail against a doctype (the support-desk pattern: mail to support@ creating Issue records). Where the business uses this: the same identity and custody rules, plus a named owner for the receiving doctype's queue, because an inbound channel nobody reads is worse than none — senders believe they have been heard.

Practical rule: send the identity test after any mail change — one email from the site to an external mailbox at a major provider, and confirm it arrives in the inbox, sender displayed correctly. Thirty seconds; it is the difference between configured and working.

lessons.title: Chapter 5 — The Email Queue
lessons.html:
Open Email Queue (awesome bar). Every outbound email the site generates passes through this list on its way out, and the queue is the channel's health instrument.

Reading the queue. Each row is one email with its status:

• Not Sent — generated, awaiting dispatch. A handful, briefly, is normal traffic; a growing pile is the alarm.
• Sending / Sent — in flight / delivered to the mail service.
• Error — dispatch failed, with the error recorded on the row. The error text is the diagnosis: authentication failures point at credentials (Chapter 4's rotation note), connection failures at the mail service or its settings, rejection messages at the recipient side or deliverability.

The daily glance (module 1's calendar line). Thirty seconds: the queue's recent rows scanned for Error status and for a Not Sent pile that is not draining. The stakes justify the ritual: the queue carries business documents — invoices to customers, statements from the monthly run, purchase orders to suppliers, the compliance calendar's Notification reminders. A stuck queue is all of those silently not arriving, and nothing else in the system will mention it.

The stuck-queue procedure.

1. Read the newest errors — the error text names the family (credential, connection, rejection).
2. Fix the cause: the rotated-but-not-updated password corrected on the Email Account record; the mail-service settings re-verified; the deliverability problem escalated to the domain custodian.
3. Confirm the drain: queued mail retries; watch Not Sent convert to Sent. Where rows aged beyond usefulness (the reminder for a meeting past), the business decision is made deliberately: send late or cancel, and for customer-facing documents late is almost always right — the invoice must arrive.
4. The identity test (Chapter 4) as the closing check.
5. Log the incident with cause and duration — a queue that sticks twice for the same cause is a process fault (the rotation procedure missing its update step, usually).

The volume read. Beside errors, the queue's volume tells stories: the statement run's monthly spike confirms it fired (the absence of the spike is the finding); an unexplained surge points at a misconfigured Notification looping (Chapter 6's standing caution); near-zero traffic on a site that should hum means senders are failing upstream.

Practical rule: after any mail-related change — credentials, Email Account settings, the provider's side — the queue is watched through one natural send. Configured is not working; the queue draining is working.

lessons.title: Chapter 6 — Notifications and Auto Email Reports
lessons.html:
Two doctypes turn the email channel into the programme's reminder and reporting machinery — the "set system Notifications against the dates" line that every track's calendar has been assuming is built here.

The Notification doctype. Open Notification (awesome bar) > New. Each record is one automated message rule:

• The document type and event — on save, on submit, on cancel, on a value change, or — the calendar workhorse — days before or after a date field (three days before a Purchase Order's expected date; on the compliance calendar's filing dates via their carrying doctype).
• The condition — the filter that scopes the rule (only submitted documents, only where a status field says so, only above a value). The condition discipline is the chapter's core caution: an unscoped notification is spam at machine scale, and spam teaches recipients to ignore the channel — after which the notification that matters dies in the same ignored folder.
• The recipients — by role, by a field on the document (the document's owner, the assigned user), or fixed addresses. Prefer roles and document fields to named people: the notification wired to a person breaks at their leaving; wired to a role it survives (module 2's access-follows-the-job, applied to mail).
• The message — subject and body, with the document's fields available as placeholders; the document link included so the recipient lands one click from action.

The notification register. Every active Notification is a channel register line: purpose, owner, recipients, last reviewed. The annual review reads them all — the notification for the process that no longer exists is retired, and the one nobody remembers requesting gets the module 5 archaeology. The looping notification (a rule that fires on save and edits that trigger saves) is the classic incident; the queue's volume read (Chapter 5) is what catches it.

The Auto Email Report doctype. Open Auto Email Report: a saved report, emailed on a schedule — daily, weekly, monthly — to named recipients, with filters fixed and the format chosen. This is the push layer over module 1's report machinery, and its lawful uses are the standing reads the tracks defined: the branch P&L to each branch manager monthly, the aged receivables to the collections owner weekly, the draft-documents list to the close owner on day one.

The same two rules govern: recipients by role/need (the report to someone who never opens it is noise plus a data-exposure surface — the report email carries business data into mailboxes, so the recipient list is a permission decision), and the register line with an annual review that retires the unread.

Practical rule: the test for every automated message is the recipient's verdict, asked annually: do you act on this? Keep the ones that move work; retire the rest. A lean automated channel is one people actually read.

lessons.title: Chapter 7 — Integrations and credential custody
lessons.html:
An integration is another system connected to the site — reading it, writing to it, or both. Each one is a door, and doors get the module's full treatment.

The standing example. The e-invoicing rail: ZhiftERP transmits invoices to the tax authority through the NGE Portal integration (the tax module's compliance machinery). It carries every property this chapter governs: an external endpoint, a credential, a data flow of consequence, a failure mode (invoices not transmitting) that is silent locally and loud legally, and a health check the business must own. Payment gateways, SMS gateways (the SMS Settings page where the business sends transactional SMS), and any partner system connected by API follow the same pattern.

Credentials — the custody rules. Integration credentials are keys to the business's data, and they concentrate the module's risk:

1. Issued minimal: where the platform supports API keys per user (the API Access section on the User record generates a key/secret pair), the integration gets its own dedicated user with exactly the roles its function needs (module 2's least-privilege applied to machines) — never a person's credentials, and never a System Manager's. The integration user is named for its function (nge-portal-integration), fenced like any user, and visible in every access review.
2. Stored in custody: the business's credential store — not chat history, not a spreadsheet, not one person's head. Access to the store: the sysadmin and backstop, listed.
3. Rotated on the calendar and at events: the security calendar's rotation line (module 8), plus immediate rotation when a holder leaves or exposure is suspected — and the rotation updates both ends (the store and the connected system's configuration), or Chapter 5's stuck-queue lesson repeats with a different channel.
4. Revoked when the integration retires: the dead integration's live credential is a door with no doorman; retirement is a checklist (credential revoked, user disabled, register entry closed).

The data-flow question, asked at connection time. Before any integration connects: what data flows out, what flows in, and who approved that flow? The answer goes in the register entry — because "what does this integration actually see?" is a question the business will eventually be asked (by an auditor, a customer, or its own owner), and connection time is when the answer is cheap.

Practical rule: count the doors quarterly — the integration register's entries against the actual API-enabled users and connected apps on the site. A door not in the register is the finding; module 5's reconciliation logic, applied to connections.

lessons.title: Chapter 8 — The integration register & the HealthTrade case
lessons.html:
The integration register — the channel inventory's heaviest section. Per integration, one entry:

1. What and why — the system, the business purpose, the data flow in both directions.
2. The owner — the person who answers "do we still need this" and receives its failures.
3. The credential — which dedicated user, where the secret lives, last rotated.
4. The health check — the specific read that proves it is working, and its cadence: for the e-invoicing rail, the transmitted-invoices confirmation the tax module's routine expects; for a gateway, the last successful transaction's recency.
5. The failure mode and response — what silence looks like, who is told, what the workaround is (the runbook's scenario 4 logic, per channel).

The monthly integration line (module 1's calendar) walks the register's health checks; the quarterly door count (Chapter 7) reconciles it against reality.

The HealthTrade case — the channels year.

The identity move (Chapter 4). The ground: all system mail leaving from a personal free-mail address the old implementation era configured. The move runs as a project: the domain's mail authentication set up with the domain custodian, the Email Account record rebuilt on accounts@ the business domain, Default Outgoing set, credential into custody, the identity test passed to three external providers — and the next monthly statement run lands in inboxes. Collections notices two replies in the first week from customers who had never been receiving the statements: the old identity had been decorating spam folders for months. The deliverability lesson writes itself into the register.

The stuck queue, closed properly (Chapter 5). Module 1's month-three catch — the stuck email queue — gets its root cause on this module's procedure: Error rows naming authentication failure; the cause, a well-meant password rotation that never reached the Email Account record; the fix, the record updated, the queue drained, 41 queued documents sent late-but-sent (the customer-facing rule), and the rotation procedure amended with its update-both-ends step. The incident log's closing line becomes the training example.

The reminder layer built (Chapter 6). The compliance calendar's dates get their Notifications (days-before rules, recipients by role), the close owner gets the day-one draft-documents Auto Email Report, and the branch P&L mails monthly to each manager. The first annual do-you-act-on-this review retires 5 of 17 automated messages — the lean channel principle applied.

The doors counted (Chapters 7-8). The register is built: the NGE Portal e-invoicing integration (dedicated integration user, credential into custody, the transmitted-invoices health check joining the monthly line) and the SMS gateway (same treatment). The first quarterly door count finds one undocumented API key on a former consultant's user — revoked the same day, the user long disabled but the key never was; the leaver checklist gains its "and API keys" line. The MD's note: the system's mouths and doors now have names on them.

lessons.title: Chapter 9 — Common mistakes & the sixth law
lessons.html:
The channel layer's recurring failures, then the review list.

Pattern 1 — the personal-mailbox identity. Symptom: system mail from a free-mail or personal address; statements in spam folders; the sent history leaving with a person. Cause: the identity rule unknown at setup (Chapter 4). Fix: the domain identity project — authentication with the domain custodian, the Email Account rebuilt, custody, the identity test — and the deliverability payoff measured at the next statement run.

Pattern 2 — the silent queue. Symptom: documents "sent" for weeks that never arrived; collections weakening; the discovery made by an annoyed customer. Cause: the queue never read (Chapter 5). Fix: the daily thirty-second glance, the stuck-queue procedure, and the volume read that confirms the big runs fired.

Pattern 3 — notification spam. Symptom: automated mail everyone ignores; the important alert dead in the same folder; a looping rule flooding the queue. Cause: unscoped conditions and unreviewed rules (Chapter 6). Fix: the condition discipline at creation, recipients by role, the register with its annual do-you-act-on-this review, and the queue's volume read as the loop alarm.

Pattern 4 — the hard-typed format. Symptom: the invoice showing a bank account the business closed two years ago; identity details that survived three reprints of reality. Cause: business data typed into print formats instead of printing from records (Chapters 2-3). Fix: the rule — fields from the document, identity from the letterhead, nothing hard-typed — enforced by the specimen review, and the offending formats corrected through module 5's lane.

Pattern 5 — the credential in someone's head. Symptom: the integration only one person can fix; the rotation that breaks the channel because only one end was updated; the leaver who takes the mail password with them. Cause: custody never established (Chapters 4, 7). Fix: the credential store with its access list, dedicated integration users at least privilege, rotation with the update-both-ends step, and the leaver checklist's credential lines.

Pattern 6 — the unregistered door. Symptom: an API key nobody can explain; an integration discovered during an incident; the dead connection with the live credential. Cause: doors opened without register entries (Chapters 7-8). Fix: the register as the connection procedure's output, the quarterly door count reconciling register to reality, and the retirement checklist closing what is no longer needed.

The review list. Before the quiz, confirm you can: state the channel rule and keep the inventory; configure Letter Head and Print Settings and run the specimen discipline; govern Print Formats by the three levels and the assignment rules; set up the domain sending identity on the Email Account record and run the identity test; read the Email Queue's statuses and run the stuck-queue procedure; build scoped Notifications and Auto Email Reports with recipients by role and the annual review; apply the four credential custody rules with dedicated integration users; and keep the integration register with its health checks and the quarterly door count.

The sixth law: every channel has an owner, an identity the business controls, a credential under custody, and a health read on the calendar — silence is a finding, not a comfort. Module 7 covers monitoring and the health reads.
