monitoring_health.title: Sysadmin 7 — Monitoring, Performance & the Health Reads
monitoring_health.desc: Monitoring in ZhiftERP: the three reading rules (trend not point, exception not census, silence is a finding); the Error Log triage and its four patterns; the Scheduled Job Type/Log pulse check with the all-jobs-silent diagnosis; Background Jobs as the on-demand instrument with the three user-facing translations; the weekly people-read with its privacy posture; storage and reference-timing trends with evidenced escalation; the one-page health page and the three assembled cadences; and the incident log with its quarterly cause read.

lessons.title: Chapter 1 — The system is read before it is felt
lessons.html:
This module covers monitoring: the Error Log, the scheduler and its job logs, the background job queue, the login and activity reads, storage and performance trends, the health page that assembles them, and the incident log that closes the loop.

The principle. Every system state that matters can be discovered two ways: read from the system's own instruments while it is small, or felt by the business when it is large — the backup that quietly stopped, felt at the restore; the scheduler that died, felt when the accruals never posted; the storage that filled, felt when attachments start failing at month-end. Monitoring is choosing to read. Every instrument in this module already exists on the site; the module's work is the habit — the reads on the calendar, the numbers trended, the exceptions investigated.

The three reading rules.

1. Trend, not point. A single number means little; its direction means everything. Storage at 60% is a fact; storage that moved 40 → 50 → 60 in three months is a forecast. The health page (Chapter 7) exists to hold last month's numbers beside this month's.
2. Exception, not census. The reads are built to surface what changed — new error types, jobs that stopped, counts that jumped — not to re-read the unchanged. A five-minute daily read stays five minutes only if it is exception-shaped.
3. Silence is a finding. The statement run's queue spike that did not happen, the nightly backup that is not listed, the scheduler log with no entries since Tuesday — the absence of expected activity is the loudest signal in this module, and the one untrained readers miss, because nothing looks wrong.

The escalation posture. Monitoring feeds two lanes: the site-custody findings the sysadmin fixes (a misconfigured notification looping, a permission error pattern), and the platform-custody findings raised to CloudERP.One with evidence — the five-item report of module 1, now armed with this module's instruments: the exact Error Log entries, the job log timestamps, the trend numbers. Monitoring is what turns "the system is slow" into a report the host can act on in one pass.

Module contents. Chapter 2: the Error Log. Chapter 3: the scheduler and its logs. Chapter 4: background jobs and the queues. Chapter 5: logins, lockouts, and the Activity Log. Chapter 6: storage and performance trends. Chapter 7: the health page and the assembled reads. Chapter 8: the incident log and the HealthTrade case. Chapter 9: review and the law.

lessons.title: Chapter 2 — The Error Log
lessons.html:
Open Error Log (awesome bar). Every unhandled failure inside the site writes an entry here — the site's own complaint channel, and the daily read's first stop.

Reading an entry. Each record carries the timestamp, the method or context that failed, and the traceback — the technical text describing where and why. The sysadmin does not need to program to read it usefully; three fields carry the triage:

• The first and last lines of the traceback — the error's name and its immediate cause, often plain enough ("PermissionError", a missing value, a timeout).
• The method/context — which machinery failed: a report, a notification, a scheduled job, a document event.
• The count and clustering — one entry is an event; forty identical entries since 9am is a pattern with a start time, and the start time usually names the cause (what changed at 9am?).

The triage, as a procedure.

1. New or known? The daily read scans for error types not seen before. Known noise — the benign entries every site accumulates — is recognised and passed; a new type is investigated the day it appears, because day one it has a fresh trail and day thirty it has folklore.
2. Site custody or platform custody? The custody map's question, asked with better evidence now: a permission error on one user is module 2's territory; a repeating failure inside platform machinery is a raise — with the entry's full text copied whole into the five-item report (the error text is the single highest-value item a support report carries).
3. User-facing or silent? An error a user saw has a person to follow up with; an error nobody saw is this module's speciality — the failing notification, the dying import — found here or not at all.

The patterns worth memorising.

• The 9am cluster — errors starting when a change deployed: module 5's verify-live step missed something; the change lane's log names the suspect.
• The nightly regular — the same entry every night at the same minute: a scheduled job failing on schedule (Chapter 3 confirms which).
• The permission drizzle — scattered PermissionErrors from one role after a permission change: the change was too tight; module 2's diagnosis path.
• The integration silence-with-errors — the channel register's health check failing while its errors accumulate here: Chapter 6-of-module-6's procedures, with the entries as evidence.

Practical rule: the Error Log read is sixty seconds when clean — filter to the last day, scan the types, done. Its value compounds through the calendar: the sysadmin who reads daily recognises "new" on sight, which is the entire skill.

lessons.title: Chapter 3 — The scheduler and its logs
lessons.html:
Half the programme's automation runs on the scheduler — the machinery that fires time-based work: the nightly backups, the Auto Repeat entries (the Accounts track's monthly rent journal), the Notifications on their date rules, the Auto Email Reports, the statement run's schedule, the queue's dispatch. A dead or limping scheduler silently stops all of it at once, which makes this chapter's read the daily list's most consequential thirty seconds.

The instruments.

• Scheduled Job Type (awesome bar) — the catalogue: every scheduled job the site knows, with its frequency and whether it is stopped. The read here is the census — what should be running.
• Scheduled Job Log — the record: each job's executions with status and time. The read here is the pulse — what actually ran, and when it last did.

The daily pulse check. Open the Scheduled Job Log, sorted newest first: entries from the last few minutes and hours confirm the scheduler lives. Then the two exception reads:

1. Failures: filter to failed status in the last day — each failure is an Error Log companion entry (Chapter 2's nightly-regular pattern lands here); repeated failure of one job is a raise or a fix depending on custody.
2. Silence: the last-execution ages. A job that should run hourly showing a last run of Tuesday is the finding — and if all jobs show Tuesday, the scheduler itself died Tuesday, and everything time-based has been off since: backups, reminders, queues. That discovery is a same-day, highest-severity raise — and the reason this read is daily, because every day undetected multiplies the recovery: the missed Auto Repeats to post manually, the queued documents to drain, the backup gap to acknowledge in the continuity log.

The business-side verification. The logs prove the machinery ran; the tracks prove the work arrived — and both checks exist because each catches what the other misses:

• The Accounts close confirms the Auto Repeat entries posted (checklist line 2 — "confirmed fired").
• The queue's volume read confirms the statement run's spike (module 6).
• The backup presence check confirms the nightly set (module 4).

When a track-side check fails ("the rent journal didn't post"), this chapter is the diagnosis path: the Scheduled Job Log says whether the machinery ran; the Error Log says why not; the custody map says who fixes it.

Practical rule: after any platform update or incident recovery, the pulse check runs immediately even though it is "not time" — schedulers are the classic casualty of disturbed systems, and the thirty-second read is cheaper than discovering it at month-end.

lessons.title: Chapter 4 — Background jobs and the queues
lessons.html:
Beside the clock-driven scheduler, the site runs background jobs — work handed off to run behind the interface so the user is not held waiting: the large report, the bulk import's processing, the heavy document submissions, the email dispatch. This chapter is reading that machinery.

The instrument. Open the Background Jobs page (awesome bar): the current queues with their jobs — queued, started, and failed — and each job's method and age. The healthy picture is a short, fast-moving list: jobs appear, run, vanish. The unhealthy pictures:

• The growing queue — jobs arriving faster than they finish: the site is under load or a worker has stalled. Users feel this as "the system is slow" and "my import is stuck"; the queue read converts the feeling into evidence (how many jobs, how old, which methods) for the raise.
• The failed cluster — failed jobs naming one method: the Error Log holds the why (Chapter 2's companion pattern); the fix follows custody.
• The stuck head — one long-running job blocking a queue: the age column names it; the raise carries it.

The user-facing translations. Three standing situations where this page answers the front line:

1. "My import has been running forever." The import's processing is a background job — find it: still running (patience, with an age estimate), failed (the Data Import document carries the error rows; module 3's procedure), or absent (it never queued — resubmit).
2. "The report never loads." Heavy reports queue in the background; a queue backlog delays them all. The read distinguishes "this report is heavy" (one job, running) from "the site is congested" (many jobs, aging) — two different escalations.
3. "Emails are delayed." The email dispatch rides this machinery too — the Email Queue (module 6) shows the documents; this page shows whether the machinery that drains it is moving. The pair together diagnose in one minute what either alone only suspects.

Where it sits in the calendar. Not a standing daily line — the daily read's instruments (Error Log, Scheduled Job Log, Email Queue, backup presence) catch the failures that matter overnight. Background Jobs is the on-demand instrument: opened when slowness is reported, when an import stalls, when the queue is suspected — plus a weekly glance riding the performance read (Chapter 6) so its normal picture stays familiar. An instrument read only during incidents is read badly; the weekly glance is what keeps "normal" recognisable.

Practical rule: every "the system is slow" report gets this page opened while the slowness is live — the evidence evaporates with the queue. A screenshot of the live queue state is worth three paragraphs in the raise.

lessons.title: Chapter 5 — Logins, lockouts, and the Activity Log
lessons.html:
Who is using the system, from where, and who is failing to — the people-side reads, sitting between this module and module 8's security layer.

The instruments.

• The User list's last-login read (module 2 introduced it): Enabled users sorted by last login. The two ends carry the findings — never-logged-in accounts (granted but unused: a joiner who never started, or an account created for no one) and the ninety-day-quiet accounts the quarterly recertification disables.
• The Activity Log (awesome bar): the stream of logins and significant actions, filterable by user and time. The read is exception-shaped: failed login clusters (many failures on one account: a forgotten password if the owner confirms, a guessing attempt if not — the lockout setting from module 1's settings walk is the automatic answer, and the cluster is the read that proves it fired), off-hours patterns (logins at hours the job does not explain — a conversation, not an accusation: legitimate reasons abound, but the pattern is read, not ignored), and the after-event reconstruction (when module 8's audit questions arrive — who was in the system Tuesday evening — this log is the first answer).

The weekly read (module 1's calendar line, now fully specified).

1. Failed-login clusters in the last week: each cluster attributed (owner confirms the fumble) or escalated (module 8's security-event response for the unexplained).
2. Lockouts fired: read as the control working; repeated lockouts on one account get the owner conversation (training or trouble).
3. The user delta (module 2's read) — the same sitting, the same five minutes.

The session angle. Module 1's settings walk set session expiry; this read verifies the policy is livable: complaints about constant re-login mean the expiry is too tight for the work pattern (a governed settings conversation, not a silent loosening), while sessions that never seem to end mean the setting drifted or a change reverted it — the annual walk's reconciliation catches the second; the complaints catch the first.

The privacy posture, stated once. These reads exist to protect the system and its users — the honest account holder is defended by the log that shows their account guessed-at and locked, exactly as the honest cashier is defended by the till count. The reads are performed by the named sysadmin, on the calendar, for the written purposes; browsing colleagues' activity outside the reads is itself an access-review finding. The instrument that guards the system is governed like everything else that touches it.

Practical rule: the weekly people-read is five minutes because it is exception-shaped — clusters, lockouts, deltas. The month it takes twenty minutes is the month something is happening; that is the read working.

lessons.title: Chapter 6 — Storage and performance trends
lessons.html:
The slow-growing numbers: disk and speed. Neither fails suddenly — both drift, which makes them the purest case for the trend-not-point rule.

Storage. The site's footprint is the database plus the files (module 4's two components, now read as sizes). The platform exposes the numbers through the host's panel or the support channel; the sysadmin records them monthly on the health page — database size, files size, and the deltas.

• The reads: steady growth proportional to trading is health; a delta jump names an event (a heavy import month, an attachment-happy new process, a runaway log) — identified while it is one month old, not archaeologised at 90% full.
• The attachment economy: files usually outgrow the database, because evidence habits (this programme's own doing) attach documents everywhere. The governance is sizing, not abstinence: module 1's settings walk set the attachment size limit; scans are made at document resolution, not photo resolution; and the occasional bulk offender (the 40MB video someone attached to a delivery note) is found by asking the host for the largest-files read when a jump appears.
• The forecast conversation: the trend line answers "when do we need more" months ahead, which converts a storage crisis into a plan-and-budget line with the host.

Performance. Speed has no single gauge; the read is assembled:

1. The user-report channel, disciplined: "slow" reports are logged with the what/when/where (which screen, which report, what time, how many users) — the pattern across reports is the instrument. One person's slow afternoon is noise; everyone's slow month-end mornings is a signal with a shape.
2. The reference timings: a small set of standing operations timed monthly — the Trial Balance for the current month, one heavy standard report, one list view of the busiest doctype — the same operations, the same filters, logged on the health page. Drift across months is the evidence that survives the "it feels slower" argument in both directions.
3. The background-jobs glance (Chapter 4) riding the same monthly sitting.

The escalation, evidenced. Performance raises to the host carry: the reference-timing trend, the pattern from the user reports (times, screens, concurrency), and the live-state evidence where captured. That package lets the host act in one pass — resource sizing, query attention, whatever the platform side needs — instead of a week of "can you describe the slowness".

Practical rule: both numbers are boring by design — two lines on the health page, five minutes monthly. The boredom is the point: the month either line becomes interesting, it does so with three months of context already attached.

lessons.title: Chapter 7 — The health page and the assembled reads
lessons.html:
The module's instruments assemble into one page and three cadences. This chapter is the assembly — the reads module 1's calendar promised, now fully built.

The health page. One page, kept with the ops log, holding the standing numbers month by month:

• Storage: database size, files size, deltas (Chapter 6).
• The reference timings (Chapter 6).
• Error Log: new types this month, and the noise register (the known-benign list that keeps the daily read fast).
• Scheduler: failures this month, and any silence incidents.
• Email: queue error count, and the big runs confirmed (the statement spike).
• Users: enabled count, System Manager count (always two), lockouts, ninety-day-quiet count.
• Backups: presence-check misses (target zero), the drill's minutes (module 4's RTO evidence).
• Incidents: count by custody, with repeat-cause flags (Chapter 8).

Twelve columns a year. The page's value is the row beside last month's row — every trend rule in this module lands here.

The daily read (five minutes), assembled:

1. Error Log — last day, new types (Chapter 2).
2. Scheduled Job Log — the pulse and the failures (Chapter 3).
3. Email Queue — errors and the drain (module 6).
4. Backup presence (module 4).

The weekly read (ten minutes): the people-read — failed-login clusters, lockouts, the user delta (Chapter 5) — plus the Background Jobs familiarity glance (Chapter 4).

The monthly read (thirty minutes): the health page's row filled — storage, timings, the counts — the restore drill (module 4), the integration health checks (module 6), and the incident log's month read (Chapter 8). The row's anomalies each get one line of cause or one open action.

Delegation and continuity. The reads are procedures with owners, which means they delegate: the daily read is an ideal early responsibility for the sysadmin's backstop (module 1's design) — it builds the recognise-normal skill that every other duty needs, and it means the reads survive leave and departure. The health page itself is the handover test's monitoring chapter: a newcomer reading twelve months of rows knows the system's normal better than most incumbents who never wrote it down.

Practical rule: resist adding numbers to the page. Every number must have a reader and a rule (what makes it a finding); a page of forty unowned metrics is a dashboard nobody reads, and the five-minute daily read stays five minutes only because the page stayed one page.

lessons.title: Chapter 8 — The incident log & the HealthTrade case
lessons.html:
The incident log. Every finding that required action — from any module — closes with a log entry: what, when detected, how detected (which read — the instrument's credit matters, Chapter 9 explains why), custody, cause, fix, duration, and the follow-up if any. The log's two standing reads:

• Monthly: the month's incidents counted by custody for the health page.
• Quarterly (module 1's calendar): the read by cause — the same cause twice is a process fault, and the fix moves upstream: the procedure amended, the checklist line added, the setting corrected. The quarterly read is where incidents stop repeating, which is the log's entire purpose.

The HealthTrade case — the monitoring year.

The reads installed. The daily five-minute read starts in module 1's month three; this module completes the set: the health page opens with its first row (storage recorded from the host's numbers, the three reference timings logged — Trial Balance 4 seconds, the stock report 11, the invoice list 2), the noise register is built in the first fortnight (six known-benign error types listed, after which the daily Error Log scan drops to its promised sixty seconds), and the weekly and monthly sittings take their calendar slots.

The scheduler death, caught same-day (Chapter 3). A Thursday daily read finds the Scheduled Job Log's newest entry aged nine hours — the pulse check's all-jobs-silent picture. Raised same-day at incident severity with the log timestamps; the host restores the scheduler by afternoon; the recovery checklist runs: the backup presence check confirms the night's set must be watched (the next nightly lands normally), two Auto Repeat entries that missed their slot are posted through the close's confirmed-fired line, and the queue drains its held mail. The incident log entry credits the read: detected by daily pulse check, nine hours after failure; prior detection method: month-end, twenty days away. The entry becomes the case for the calendar the next time anyone calls the daily read bureaucratic.

The slow month-end, escalated with evidence (Chapter 6). Three users report slowness in the same close week; the discipline turns it into a package: the reports logged with times and screens (all morning, all report-heavy), the reference timings re-run mid-slowness (the stock report at 31 seconds against its 11-second baseline), the Background Jobs screenshot showing the aged queue. The raise lands with the host in one pass; the platform side resizes the site's resources; the next close's timings return to baseline — and the health page's timing row carries the whole story in three numbers: 11, 31, 12.

The storage jump, named in a month (Chapter 6). Month five's files delta triples. The largest-files read from the host names the cause inside a day: a new branch process attaching full-resolution photos to every goods receipt. The fix is process, not storage: the scan-resolution guidance lands at the branch, the attachment size limit is confirmed doing its job, and the delta returns to trend. The quarterly incident read later flags nothing — one cause, one occurrence, closed.

The MD's line for the year file: the system now tells us about its problems before we feel them — and the page proves it.

lessons.title: Chapter 9 — Common mistakes & the seventh law
lessons.html:
The monitoring layer's recurring failures, then the review list.

Pattern 1 — the unread instruments. Symptom: the Error Log opened for the first time during an incident, holding six months of the answer; the scheduler dead for weeks; every failure felt before it is read. Cause: the instruments exist and the habit does not (Chapter 1). Fix: the three cadences installed with owners — the reads are minutes precisely because they are regular — and the incident log's how-detected field building the case that keeps them funded.

Pattern 2 — the census read. Symptom: monitoring that takes an hour and gets skipped; dashboards of forty metrics nobody owns; the important exception buried in the unchanged. Cause: reads built as censuses instead of exceptions (Chapters 1, 7). Fix: exception-shaping — new types, deltas, silences — the noise register keeping the known out of the way, and the one-page rule on the health page.

Pattern 3 — the ignored silence. Symptom: the missing backup nobody missed; the statement spike that did not happen; the job log quiet since Tuesday — all invisible because nothing looked wrong. Cause: reads that only scan for red (Chapter 1's third rule untaught). Fix: the expected-activity checks built into the reads — presence, pulse, spike — each one an absence made loud.

Pattern 4 — the evidence-free escalation. Symptom: "the system is slow" raised with heat and nothing else; the host's week of diagnostic ping-pong; the slowness gone before it is measured. Cause: escalation without instruments (Chapters 4, 6). Fix: the discipline — live-state captures while the problem is live, reference timings for the drift argument, the five-item report armed with log entries — turning every raise into a one-pass action.

Pattern 5 — the repeating incident. Symptom: the same failure quarterly, fixed the same way, surprising everyone each time. Cause: incidents closed without the log, or logged without the quarterly cause read (Chapter 8). Fix: the log as every finding's closing step, and the quarterly read moving fixes upstream — procedure, checklist, setting — until the cause stops producing.

Pattern 6 — the person-shaped monitor. Symptom: monitoring that lives in one person's habits and dies with their leave; the backstop who has never run the daily read. Cause: reads as personal practice instead of owned procedure (Chapter 7). Fix: the reads written as procedures, the daily read delegated to the backstop as their standing apprenticeship, and the health page carrying the system's "normal" on paper where the handover test can find it.

The review list. Before the quiz, confirm you can: state the three reading rules and the two escalation lanes; triage an Error Log entry — new/known, custody, seen/silent — and name the four patterns; run the scheduler pulse check and its silence diagnosis, and the business-side verifications; read Background Jobs and translate the three user-facing situations; run the weekly people-read with its privacy posture; keep the storage and timing trends and build an evidenced escalation; assemble the health page and the three cadences with the one-page rule; and keep the incident log with its quarterly cause read.

The seventh law: the system is read before it is felt — numbers trended, exceptions investigated, and silence treated as a finding. Module 8 closes the track: security, audit, and structure.

advanced_sysadmin.title: Sysadmin 8 — Advanced Sysadmin: Security, Audit & Structure
advanced_sysadmin.desc: Security and audit in ZhiftERP: the five layers and the honest threat picture; the completed password/session layer with the lost-device path; the two-factor rollout with method policy, written recovery procedure, and coverage read; the Version trail's three disciplines with track-changes confirmed on governed doctypes; the Deleted Document review and access-log reads; the security calendar and the six-section annual review; the six-step incident response with containment first; and the structural close — the handover and absence tests, and the track's eight laws.

lessons.title: Chapter 1 — The security layers
lessons.html:
This final module covers security and audit: proving identity (passwords and two-factor), the audit trail (the Version history, the Activity and access logs, the Deleted Document list), the security calendar, the annual review, incident response, and the structural close — the handover test and the track's eight laws.

The layered design. No single control secures a system; the design is layers, each catching what the previous missed — and the sysadmin's competence is knowing which layer answers which threat:

1. Identity — is this login really its person? Passwords enforced by policy, two-factor authentication, session controls (Chapters 2-3).
2. Authorisation — may this person do this? Module 2's entire machinery: roles, profiles, fences, the recertification. This module recaps it only as a layer in the stack.
3. Audit — what happened, by whom, when? The trail that deters, detects, and reconstructs (Chapters 4-5).
4. Custody — credentials, backups, and channels under named control: modules 4 and 6, recapped as layers.
5. Structure — the function surviving its people: the calendar, the review, the handover test (Chapters 6-8).

The threat picture, honestly sized. A trading business's real threats are ranked by frequency, and the ranking should drive the effort:

• The careless everyday — shared passwords, phishing clicks, the leaver's live login, the credential in a chat: the overwhelming majority, and every one answered by discipline already built in this track.
• The insider opportunity — the over-mighty account, the unwatched adjustment power: module 2's separations and this module's audit trail are the answer pair.
• The outside attack — credential guessing and stolen passwords: the lockout (module 1's settings), two-factor (Chapter 3), and the platform's own defences (the host's layer).

The exotic attack scenarios that dominate security conversation are the host's professional territory; the site's layer defends against the threats that actually arrive, which are the boring ones above.

Module contents. Chapter 2: passwords and sessions, completed. Chapter 3: two-factor authentication and its rollout. Chapter 4: the audit trail — Versions and track-changes. Chapter 5: the access logs and the Deleted Document review. Chapter 6: the security calendar and the annual review. Chapter 7: security incident response. Chapter 8: the HealthTrade close and the structural tests. Chapter 9: the track's laws.

lessons.title: Chapter 2 — Passwords and sessions, completed
lessons.html:
Module 1's settings walk set the password and session policy; this chapter completes the layer with the practices around the settings.

The password stack, recapped and finished.

• The enforced minimum: System Settings' password strength requirement — the policy users cannot decline. Already set at the walk; verified at the annual review.
• The lockout: consecutive-failure lockout with its window — the automatic answer to guessing, whose firing Chapter 5-of-module-7's weekly read observes.
• The reset flow: self-service, logged, and the only lane — the admin never sets or knows a user's password (module 2's rule). The reset flow is also the standing phishing target, which is Chapter 3's strongest argument: a stolen password meets a second factor.
• The human layer: the three teachable rules that survive training — passwords are individual (module 2's first mortal sin), never typed anywhere but the site's own login page (the phishing defence in one sentence), and never sent, stored, or requested by anyone including the sysadmin (the social-engineering defence in one more).

Sessions, completed.

• Expiry per the settings walk — hours, livability verified by module 7's read.
• The active-sessions view: a user's sessions are visible and revocable — the tool for the lost-device afternoon: the user reports the phone gone, the sessions are revoked, the password reset, and two-factor (Chapter 3) means the finder holds nothing useful. Minutes, on a written path.
• Simultaneous-session policy: where the platform exposes limits, the decision is written like every setting; where it does not, the Activity Log's patterns (module 7) are the compensating read.

The privileged accounts, one notch stricter. The two System Managers (module 2's rule) carry the strictest hygiene: the strongest passwords, two-factor first and mandatory (Chapter 3's rollout order), and their sessions the first reviewed after any suspicious event — because the account that can change everything is the account worth stealing.

Devices, one paragraph of honesty. The site is reached from browsers on machines the sysadmin does not manage. The site-side compensations are exactly the layers above — expiry that limits a stolen session's life, two-factor that limits a stolen password's worth, the revocation path for the lost device — plus the one device rule worth teaching: the shared or public machine gets a logout, not a closed tab. The rest of device security belongs to the business's general IT hygiene, named in the security policy so nobody believes the site's layers cover what they cannot.

Practical rule: the password layer's health is read in one number at the annual review — the count of accounts exempted from any part of the policy. The target is zero; every exemption is a documented decision with an expiry.

lessons.title: Chapter 3 — Two-factor authentication and its rollout
lessons.html:
Two-factor authentication is the single highest-value security upgrade available to the site: it converts the stolen password — the most common real attack — from a breach into a failed login.

The mechanics. System Settings carries the two-factor switch (Enable Two Factor Auth) and its method options; enabled, each user enrols — the standard method pairs an authenticator app generating time-based codes, with the platform's supported alternatives (email or SMS OTP) available where the policy accepts them. The design decisions, made once and written:

• The method policy: the authenticator app is the strong default (codes generated on the device, no delivery channel to intercept); SMS/email OTP is the accommodation, accepted knowingly where the app is impractical.
• The scope: which users must enrol — the rollout below answers it in phases, ending at all Desk users.
• The recovery path: the lost-phone procedure, written before the first lost phone: identity verified by a defined check (not "sounds like them on the phone" — the reset request is itself a social-engineering target), the factor reset by the sysadmin, re-enrolment same day, the event logged. The recovery path is the layer's weakest point exactly because it is the bypass; it gets procedure-grade treatment.

The rollout, in phases.

1. The two System Managers first — the highest-value accounts, and the sysadmin learning the enrolment and recovery flows personally before asking anyone else to.
2. The money and adjustment powers next: Payment Entry release, the Journal Entry pen, the frozen-edit role, write-off approvers — module 2's consequential grants, each now behind a second factor.
3. All remaining Desk users, branch by branch, with the enrolment done in person or on a call (the five-minute walkthrough that prevents the week of confusion), the recovery path explained at enrolment, and the standing test at the end of each phase: the phase's users listed, enrolment confirmed, exceptions documented with expiry dates.

The coverage read. Two-factor coverage joins the health page (module 7): enrolled count against Desk-user count, target one hundred percent, exemptions listed by name with their documented reasons and expiries. The annual review (Chapter 6) walks the exemptions — an exemption that survives two reviews is a decision that needs re-making.

The resistance, answered once. The friction argument arrives on schedule: it slows login. The honest answer: seconds per session, against the alternative priced by any single credential incident — and the login that stays fast for an attacker is not a convenience, it is the vulnerability. The rollout order helps here too: when the MD and the accountant enrolled first, the argument has already lost its best advocates.

Practical rule: enrol the backstop in the recovery procedure, not just the factor — the sysadmin's own lost phone is the scenario nobody rehearses, and module 4's rule applies: the backstop executes every scenario alone.

lessons.title: Chapter 4 — The audit trail: Versions and track-changes
lessons.html:
The audit layer answers three questions about anything in the system: what happened, who did it, when. This chapter is the document-level trail; Chapter 5 adds the access-level reads.

The Version history. Doctypes with change tracking enabled write a Version record for every edit: the fields changed, the before and after values, the user, the timestamp. On any document, the timeline shows its history; the Version list (awesome bar) is the same trail searchable across documents. What this makes routine:

• The who-changed-this question — the price that moved, the credit limit that grew, the bank detail that changed on a supplier: answered in two clicks with names and times, which converts a suspicion-shaped conversation into a fact-shaped one.
• The reconstruction — a master's state at any past date, walked back through its versions: what the credit limit was when the disputed order shipped.
• The deterrence — known history changes behaviour before it records it: the quiet edit is not quiet, and everyone knowing so is half the control.

Where tracking is confirmed on. Track Changes is a per-doctype setting (visible in Customize Form); the sysadmin's job is confirming it is enabled on every doctype where history matters — the masters above all (Customer, Supplier, Item, Employee, the credit and bank-detail fields' homes), settings-like doctypes, and anywhere module 2 placed a consequential grant. The annual review (Chapter 6) includes this confirmation, because a customisation or update can disturb it and nothing visible changes until the day the history is needed and is not there.

What the trail does not cover, honestly. Transactions barely need it — the docstatus design (module 1) already forbids editing submitted documents, and Cancel/Amend keeps its own lineage. The trail's real estate is the masters and settings: the records edited in place, where change tracking is the only memory. The gap to know: reads are not versions — who looked at a record is Chapter 5's territory, and only partially; the trail records change, not curiosity.

Using the trail well — the three disciplines.

1. Ask the trail before asking people. The Version history first, the conversation second — armed, shorter, and fairer.
2. Pair it with the change lane: a Version on a governed doctype should correspond to a register entry or a documented decision (module 5's logic applied to data-shaped changes like settings) — the version without a story is the finding.
3. Never treat the trail as surveillance theatre: module 7's privacy posture applies verbatim — the trail defends the honest editor (their reasonable change has its record) and is read for causes, on procedures, by the named roles.

Practical rule: demonstrate the trail once to the management team on a harmless example — the who-changed-this answered live in two clicks. The demonstration does more for careful editing than any memo, and it teaches the owners to ask the system before asking around.

lessons.title: Chapter 5 — Access logs and the Deleted Document review
lessons.html:
The trail's second half: who entered, who touched, who removed.

The Activity Log, in its audit role. Module 7 read it for operational health (logins, failures, lockouts); the audit role adds the reconstruction use: for any event window — the disputed evening, the incident's hours — the log answers who was in the system and when, the first frame of any investigation. The read discipline is unchanged: on procedure, by the named roles, for written purposes.

The access-log family. Where the platform records document access and export events (the Access Log doctype family — exports, prints, and report downloads logged with user and time), the sysadmin knows the read exists and uses it for the questions it answers: who exported the customer list is answerable — which pairs with module 2's export-permission design: the permission governs who may; the log records who did. The honest limit from Chapter 4 stands: coverage is partial by design, and the permission layer — not the log — is the control; the log is the reconstruction aid.

The Deleted Document review — the chapter's standing procedure. The platform retains deletions: the Deleted Document list (awesome bar) records documents deleted from the site, with what, who, and when — the recycle-bin read. Its governance role is precise, because this programme's rules make deletion rare by construction:

• Transactions: Delete is off daily roles everywhere (module 2), and Cancel/Amend is the lawful correction path — so a deleted transaction is always a question.
• Masters: retirement is the Disabled checkbox (module 3) — so a deleted master with history is always a question too.

The monthly review (riding the monthly sitting):

1. Open the Deleted Document list, filtered to the month.
2. The expected residue passes: the smoke test's cleaned artifacts, the draft created in error and removed same-day by its author, the governed cleanups with their log lines.
3. Everything else gets its question: what was it, who deleted it, under what authority? An unexplained deletion of a document with any consequence is treated as an incident — the audit trail reconstructs what it was, module 2 reviews how the actor held Delete at all, and the permission is corrected.
4. The count and its exceptions join the health page: the target picture is a short list of boring rows.

Why this review carries weight beyond its minutes. Deletion is the one act that attacks the record itself — every other mischief leaves the trail intact, and the Accounts track's equity pattern named deletions as where broken books hide. The monthly read makes the site's answer structural: deletion is visible, rare, explained, and everyone knows it.

Practical rule: the review's power is its regularity, not its findings — eleven boring months are the control working. The month it is interesting, everything needed for the response is already in this module.

lessons.title: Chapter 6 — The security calendar and the annual review
lessons.html:
The layers hold because they are maintained. Two instruments: the standing calendar lines, and the annual review that walks everything once.

The security calendar (the lines this track has placed, gathered):

• Weekly: the people-read — failed-login clusters, lockouts, the user delta (module 7 / module 2).
• Monthly: the permission delta and System Manager count (module 2); the Deleted Document review (Chapter 5); two-factor coverage on the health page (Chapter 3); the integration health checks (module 6).
• Quarterly: the access recertification (module 2's strongest control); the door count reconciling the integration register (module 6); the incident log's cause read (module 7).
• At events, immediately: the leaver's same-day disable with sessions, keys, and mandate lines (modules 2, 6); credential rotation at exposure or departure (module 6); the security-event response (Chapter 7).
• Annually: the review below, plus credential rotation on schedule and the continuity full dress (module 4).

The annual security review — the walk, in one sitting scheduled across a week:

1. Settings: the System Settings security block re-walked against the recorded decisions (module 1's rule: the walk is the routine occasion for change) — password policy, lockout, session expiry, the two-factor switch.
2. Identity: two-factor coverage and its exemptions (each re-decided or expired); the policy-exemption count at its target of zero; the privileged accounts' hygiene confirmed.
3. Authorisation: the four quarterly recertifications on file; the System Manager count's twelve monthly reads all at two; the permission log's year read for unlogged changes.
4. Audit: track-changes confirmed on the governed doctypes (Chapter 4's silent-disturbance risk); the Deleted Document reviews on file; one audit-trail spot-reconstruction performed as a drill.
5. Custody: credentials rotated per schedule with both ends updated; the credential store's access list current; the integration register reconciled; backup custody confirmed (module 4's off-platform chain).
6. Structure: the runbook current with the year's amendments; the backstop's solo capability confirmed (every scenario, alone); the incident log's year read closed.

The review's output is one page: confirmations, findings with owners and dates, and the exemptions re-decided. It files beside the health page and the recertifications — the year's security posture, evidenced.

Practical rule: the review is scheduled in a quiet month, never bundled into year-end — module 7's close weeks are protected, and a review done in a rush confirms instead of examining. The calendar's whole design is that nothing here is ever urgent, because everything here is regular.

lessons.title: Chapter 7 — Security incident response
lessons.html:
Module 4's runbook holds the security scenario; this chapter completes it with the response discipline the layers make possible.

The triggers. A credential suspected exposed (the phishing click confessed, the password typed somewhere wrong, the laptop stolen); a session or login that should not exist (module 7's unexplained cluster, the off-hours pattern with no story); an insider question (the audit trail's version without a story, the unexplained deletion); an integration credential exposed (the key in a chat, the departed holder).

The response, in order — speed first, understanding second:

1. Contain: disable the affected account (reversible; waiting is not — module 4's rule verbatim), revoke its sessions, revoke its API keys where any exist. For an integration credential: rotate at both ends immediately (module 6's procedure).
2. Preserve: before anything is "tidied", the evidence is captured — the Activity Log window exported, the relevant Error Log and access entries noted, the timeline started in the incident log. Investigation needs the state as found.
3. Assess with the instruments: what could this credential reach (the account's roles and fences answer it — module 2's matrix earning its keep), and what did it touch (the Activity Log, the Version trail, the access logs, the Deleted Document list — Chapters 4-5 in their operational role). The assessment separates "exposed but unused" (the common case when containment was fast) from "used" (the escalation case).
4. Escalate on the map: platform-side involvement raised to the host at incident severity with the evidence package; business-side consequences (a touched payment path, a data exposure with legal weight) escalated to the owner and the professionals — the sysadmin runs the machinery response and never sits alone on a business-consequence decision.
5. Recover: the account re-enabled only after the cause is closed — password reset through the flow, factor re-enrolled, the user walked through what happened; the fenced re-entry beats the rushed one.
6. Learn: the incident log entry closed with cause and timeline; the quarterly read asks whether the cause is structural (the phishing click that argues for the training refresh; the shared credential that argues the custody rule harder); the runbook amended where the response found friction.

The rehearsed hour. The response above is a written procedure in the runbook with names against the steps — and the annual full dress (module 4) includes one security scenario tabletop: the stolen-laptop afternoon walked verbally, fifteen minutes, the gaps noted. The businesses that respond in minutes are the ones that have said the steps aloud before; the layers built across this track are what make minutes possible — containment is one checkbox because module 2 built identities; assessment is one matrix read because the roles are clean; the trail answers because Chapter 4 confirmed it on.

Practical rule: the response's first minute belongs to containment, not diagnosis — the instinct to "first understand what happened" is how exposure windows grow. Disable, revoke, then think; the layers guarantee the thinking has evidence waiting.

lessons.title: Chapter 8 — Case study: HealthTrade's security close & the structural tests
lessons.html:
The security layer installed, exercised, and the function proven structural. Every chapter appears.

The rollout (Chapters 2-3). The password policy was set in module 1; the completion is two-factor: Enable Two Factor Auth switched on with the authenticator-app default, the two System Managers enrolled first (the sysadmin runs the lost-phone recovery on themselves as the rehearsal), the money powers next — the MD's Payment Entry release and the accountant's journal pen behind second factors within the fortnight — then the Desk population branch by branch. Coverage joins the health page; the year closes at one hundred percent with two documented exemptions, both expiring, both re-decided at the review. The friction argument arrives on schedule from a branch manager and is answered by the rollout order: the MD enrolled three weeks ago.

The trail earns its demonstration (Chapter 4). Track-changes is confirmed on the governed doctypes (one master found silently untracked after an old customisation — corrected, and the check joins the annual review). The demonstration moment arrives unplanned: a supplier disputes their payment terms "changed without agreement" — the Version history answers in two clicks: the change, the date, the user, and the attached email that authorised it. The suspicion-shaped meeting becomes a two-minute fact check, and the management team asks for the same demonstration on the credit-limit fields the same afternoon.

The deleted-document month (Chapter 5). Month four's review finds its first interesting row: a cancelled Purchase Invoice deleted by a branch user who held Delete through a role missed in module 2's cleanup. The response runs the procedure: the trail reconstructs the document (no financial consequence — it was cancelled first), the role is corrected the same day, the permission delta logs it, and the incident entry's cause line — residual Delete grant from implementation era — feeds the quarterly read. Eleven other months: boring rows, which is the control working.

The incident tabletop (Chapter 7). The full dress includes the stolen-laptop scenario: fifteen minutes verbal, two gaps found (the after-hours contact path for the host had one name, and nobody had written where the loaner phone lives for re-enrolment) — both fixed in the runbook that week.

The structural tests (Chapter 6 and module 1's promise). The annual review runs across its week and files its page: all confirmations green, three findings closed by month-end. Then the function's own handover test: the sysadmin's documentation — the custody map, the settings records, the profiles and matrix, the registers (customisation, channel, integration), the health page, the runbook, the calendar — is handed to the backstop, who runs the function for three weeks of the sysadmin's leave: every read on schedule, one minor incident handled solo on the runbook, zero questions only the absent person could answer. The absence test passes on its first run — the same clean sheet the Accounts track's finance function scored, now on the platform beneath it. The MD's closing note: every function in this business now survives its holder — including the one that keeps the machine.

lessons.title: Chapter 9 — Common mistakes, the eighth law & the track's laws
lessons.html:
The security layer's recurring failures, the module's law, and the track's eight laws assembled.

Pattern 1 — the single-layer belief. Symptom: "we have strong passwords" as the whole security story; one control asked to do everything. Cause: the layered design unknown (Chapter 1). Fix: the five layers named with their threats — identity, authorisation, audit, custody, structure — and the annual review walking all five.

Pattern 2 — two-factor postponed. Symptom: the highest-value upgrade permanently "next quarter"; the stolen password still a breach. Cause: friction argued louder than risk (Chapter 3). Fix: the phased rollout starting at the top — System Managers, then money powers, then everyone — with coverage on the health page and exemptions that expire.

Pattern 3 — the trail assumed on. Symptom: the audit question arriving and the history not being there — track-changes silently off on the doctype that mattered. Cause: the setting assumed rather than confirmed (Chapter 4). Fix: the governed-doctype confirmation in the annual review, and the version-without-a-story read pairing the trail with the change lane.

Pattern 4 — deletion in the dark. Symptom: documents vanishing without questions; the recycle bin never opened; the record attacked at its root and nobody reading. Cause: the Deleted Document review unknown (Chapter 5). Fix: the monthly review with its expected-residue pass and everything-else-gets-a-question rule, Delete kept off daily roles, and the count on the health page.

Pattern 5 — the recovery bypass. Symptom: the strongest front door and an unlocked side gate — factor resets granted to a convincing phone voice; the reset flow socially engineered. Cause: the recovery path built casually (Chapter 3). Fix: the written recovery procedure with its defined identity check, the sysadmin and backstop rehearsed on it, and the reset events logged and reviewed.

Pattern 6 — the diagnosis-first response. Symptom: the exposed account left live while everyone investigates; the exposure window growing under discussion. Cause: understanding prioritised over containment (Chapter 7). Fix: the order taught as reflex — disable, revoke, preserve, then think — with the runbook's names against the steps and the annual tabletop keeping it said-aloud.

The review list. Before the quiz, confirm you can: name the five layers and size the real threat picture; complete the password/session layer including the lost-device path and the privileged-account notch; run the two-factor rollout with its method policy, recovery procedure, and coverage read; use the Version trail's three disciplines and confirm track-changes; run the Deleted Document review and the access-log reads with the privacy posture; walk the security calendar and the annual review's six sections; execute the six-step incident response with containment first; and run the function's own handover and absence tests.

The eighth law: security is layered and audited — identity proven, changes remembered, deletions questioned, responses rehearsed, and the function survives its holder.

The track's eight laws.

1. The platform has a named owner — every setting is a written decision, and the machinery is governed like the books it carries.
2. Access follows the job — granted by profile, fenced by record, logged as events, and removed the day the job ends.
3. Masters enter governed, once — named by the scheme, owned by name, merged never duplicated, disabled never deleted.
4. A backup untested is a hope — two custodies, complete to the file, restores rehearsed monthly, continuity written on paper.
5. Every change is staged in test, signed by its owner, deployed behind a backup, verified live, and written in the register.
6. Every channel has an owner, a controlled identity, a credential under custody, and a health read — silence is a finding.
7. The system is read before it is felt — numbers trended, exceptions investigated, silence treated as a finding.
8. Security is layered and audited — identity proven, changes remembered, deletions questioned, responses rehearsed, and the function survives its holder.

This completes the Sysadmin Professional track.
